extraction.research_question: Can computational text analysis validly measure politicians' public personality, operationalized as the agency and communion traits they project in speeches, interviews and social media posts? Which measurement strategy (supervised SVM, fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa, or zero/few-shot prompting of generative LLMs) yields the most valid measure? (Sections 1 and 3.)
extraction.theory: Brunswik (1952) lens model (Fig. 1): observers never see intrinsic personality (Y_IPT) directly; they infer it from observable personality cues X1...Xn, which are shaped by intrinsic personality and by strategic self-presentation (Y_S) (Sec. 2.2, p.3). Two problems follow: cue validity (traits are fuzzy, and some are hard to observe) and cue utilization (behaviors are equifinal/multifinal and viewers' partisan biases shape interpretation) (Sec. 2.3, pp.3-4). Trait choice: agency and communion as "meta-traits" (Bakan 1966; Hogan 1982: "get ahead" vs "get along") (Sec. 3.2.1.1, p.7). Operational definitions come from the Lechner et al. (2025) PoliPers domain-specific politician framework (15 facets): agency = Assertiveness & Will to Take Control; communion = Empathy & Compassion, positive poles only (p.7). Strong cues are direct self-statements; weak cues are indirect (p.7). Background: candidate-centered personalization (McAllister 2007; Pedersen and Rahat 2021) and congruency/heuristic accounts of voter preference (Caprara and Zimbardo 2004) (Sec. 2.1, p.3).
extraction.data: Corpus: 46 leading German politicians (leaders or co-leaders of party and/or parliamentary-group, covering all six Bundestag parties; list in Supplementary App. A), 2017-2024, spanning two full Bundestag terms (Sec. 3.1, p.5). Three sources: (1) 99 interviews with political leaders in five broadcast formats (PolInterviews dataset; Birkenmaier, Sieber and Bergstein 2025) (p.5); (2) a 300,000-post subsample of Facebook posts drawn from a raw corpus of 6.7 million politician posts (p.6); (3) German Bundestag speeches from the ParlSpeech V2 German subset (Rauh and Schwalbach 2020) (p.6). Unit of analysis: individual sentences/statements. Main corpus: a random sample of 15,000 sentences per source, so 45,000 sentences in total (implied; the text does not state the total) (p.6). Human annotation: 1,000 sentences coded by three annotators (the first author and two RAs) for agreement; a human-labeled corpus with at least 200 examples per class (agency, communion, none) for weak and strong cues (pp.7-8). Classifier evaluation set: the Fig. 3 caption reports n = 600 (balanced and unbalanced); the split is not described further in the text (p.10). Functional test set: 18 units (p.11). Partisan validation: party-level CHES expert positions (Jolly et al. 2022) for the full unlabeled corpus. US debate: transcripts of the 10 September 2024 Trump-Harris debate from the American Presidency Project, machine-translated EN to DE with the DeepL API; Trump n = 655 utterances, Harris n = 320 (p.13).
extraction.method: Measurement workflow (Fig. 2, p.6): codebook development and manual coding, then computational classification with three strategies, then validation under the ValiText framework (Birkenmaier, Wagner and Lechner 2024). Labels: agency / communion / none, with a one-sentence rationale per prediction for prompting (p.8). Strategy 1 (supervised): linear SVM on bag-of-words, following Ramey et al. (2019), with fivefold cross-validation and 80/20 splits (p.8). Strategy 2 (semisupervised): fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa base (279M parameters), threefold CV with 80/20 splits (p.8). Strategy 3 (prompting, no training): GPT-4o (proprietary), Llama 3-8B and DeepSeek-V3, each zero-shot and few-shot, with templates tailored to strong-only vs strong+weak datasets (pp.8-9). Dataset variants: strong-only vs weak+strong; balanced vs unbalanced (where "none" is twice as frequent as each trait class) (p.8). Each model run with three random seeds; metric is macro-F1 averaged across runs (pp.9-10). Validation: (a) agreement with the human test set (macro-F1; Krippendorff's alpha for human coders); (b) structural/functional tests on 18 units (6 self-report items from the Lechner et al. inventory, 6 opposing-pole items expected to be "other", 6 unrelated corpus sentences expected to be "other"); (c) sensitivity to partisan variation using party CHES positions and the debate. Results are reported only for DeepSeek-V3 in the partisan section because it was the only model to pass all earlier steps (p.12).
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. Validity is argued through convergence with human labels (macro-F1), structural functional tests, and expected correlations with ideology (CHES) and with the 2024 debate's widely reported Trump/Harris contrast (Hyatt et al. 2018). The authors state that the relative weight of intrinsic personality and strategic self-presentation in any cue cannot be determined, and say this does not matter because the goal is to automate the judgments the public would form from the cues (Sec. 2.2, p.3).
extraction.scope: Population: 46 leading German politicians (all six Bundestag parties) plus two US presidential-debate candidates. Institutions: German Bundestag (speeches and interviews) and social media. Era: 2017-2024 for German data; one debate on 10 September 2024. Language: German (the US debate was translated). Unit: sentence. Traits: only agency and communion, verbal cues only (no paraverbal, nonverbal or video). Authors position it as a feasibility and measurement-validation study, not a substantive test of drivers of personality change.

key_findings.finding: Prompt-based classification with DeepSeek-V3 is the best-performing strategy on the human-labeled test data; GPT-4o is close behind. Macro-F1 is about 0.74-0.77 across the top configurations.
key_findings.numbers: DeepSeek-V3 few-shot, strong, balanced: 0.77 (SD 0.02); DeepSeek-V3 few-shot, weak+strong, balanced: 0.76 (SD 0.01); GPT-4o few-shot, strong, balanced: 0.76 (SD 0.01); DeepSeek-V3 few-shot, strong, unbalanced: 0.77 (SD 0.01); GPT-4o few-shot, strong, unbalanced: 0.74 (SD 0.00); DeepSeek-V3 zero-shot, strong, unbalanced: 0.74 (SD 0.01)

key_findings.finding: Supervised and semisupervised baselines underperform. The SVM is best on strong balanced data; XLM-RoBERTa is best overall among the non-prompting methods. Llama 3-8B is weakest and most variable across runs.
key_findings.numbers: SVM: F1 0.63 strong balanced (large SD), 0.59 weak+strong balanced, 0.55 and 0.61 on the two unbalanced sets. XLM-RoBERTa: 0.70 strong balanced (best non-prompt result). Llama 3-8B: about 0.60 balanced and 0.55 unbalanced.

key_findings.finding: No model exceeds macro-F1 0.80. Human agreement is moderate.
key_findings.location: Sec. 4.1 and Sec. 5, p.9 and p.14; Table 1, p.10
key_findings.numbers: Krippendorff's alpha for cue presence: .73 strong, .72 weak+strong. Agency alpha .70 (strong) and .71 (weak+strong); communion .78 and .74.

key_findings.finding: Human coders mostly label sentences as no cue. Among cue sentences, communion is more common than agency.
key_findings.numbers: 'none' is 94% of strong-cue sentences and 89% of weak+strong sentences. Among cue sentences, communion is about 56% (strong) and 63% (weak+strong); agency about 44% and 38%.

key_findings.finding: Only GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 (both few-shot) pass the functional tests reliably; DeepSeek-V3 is the only model that classifies all 18 units correctly on weak+strong labels. SVM, XLM-RoBERTa and Llama 3-8B often fail to reach a 50% pass rate.
key_findings.numbers: 18 test units: 6 self-report items, 6 opposing-pole items, 6 unrelated corpus sentences. Few-shot GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 get all 18 right on strong labels; zero-shot results are described as satisfactory with minor errors.

key_findings.finding: Party-level communion tracks the left-right positions of parties on both CHES dimensions: a clear negative relation between CHES position and communion share.
key_findings.numbers: Communion share by party: LINKE 19%, Greens 12%, SPD 10%, CDU 8%, AfD and FDP about 6% each. The text reports regression lines and standard-error bars but no coefficients, N or CIs in the main text.

key_findings.finding: Agency at party level has only a weak positive link with the economic CHES dimension and none with the cultural dimension (footnote, Appendix L).
key_findings.numbers: No coefficient reported in the main text.

key_findings.finding: In the 2024 debate the measure separates the two candidates as expected: Harris shows more personality cues overall, and the agency/communion balance reverses between them.
key_findings.numbers: Personality-cue share: Harris about 23%, Trump about 10%. Trump: 63% agency / 37% communion. Harris: 59% communion / 41% agency. Utterances: Trump 655, Harris 320.

key_findings.finding: Communion is higher on social media than in interviews; agency varies less across sources. Female politicians show higher communion.
key_findings.numbers: No values reported in the main text.

key_findings.finding: Validity claim summary: prompt-based methods, particularly GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3, allow the most valid measurement; strong-only cue definitions perform better than weak+strong.
key_findings.numbers: Strong-only definitions performed better, as the authors expected; no delta is reported in the main text.

limitations: Only two traits (agency and communion) are measured; the authors call for expanding to other traits (p.15).
Verbal cues only; paraverbal and nonverbal cues (rhetoric, gesture, video, audio) are excluded; future work should be multimodal (p.15).
Sentence-level analysis only; paragraph- or token-level extensions are suggested (p.15).
Human agreement is moderate (alpha .70-.78), and no computational model exceeds macro-F1 0.80, so the ceiling on measurement precision is set by fuzzy constructs (pp.14-15).

LLM bias: generative models may reflect pretraining biases. The authors report no systematic bias in their checks but cite reports of pro-Chinese bias in DeepSeek models (Huang et al. 2025) and recommend extra validation for politically sensitive content (p.15).
Small functional-test set (n = 18) and a small debate comparison (two speakers, translated transcripts) (pp.11-13).
Partisan validation is descriptive at party level in the main text, with no reported inferential statistics; the Chapel Hill comparison relies on six parties (pp.12-13).

Self-report personality inventories are argued to be susceptible to social desirability (footnote 3, p.4); the paper treats politicians' self-reports as a kind of self-statement cue rather than intrinsic traits.
Supplementary appendices (codebook, prompts, hyperparameters, extra partisan and gender analyses) are not in the text file reviewed here, so they are unverified.
Feasibility scope: the paper argues feasibility and does not test explanatory factors for changes in displayed personality (crisis events, role transitions), which it proposes as future work (p.14).

summary_md:
Birkenmaier and Lechner ask whether a politician's *public* personality, meaning the traits they project rather than their intrinsic traits, can be measured from text. They use Brunswik's lens model: observers only ever see cues, and those cues mix true personality with strategic self-presentation. The operational definitions come from the PoliPers framework. Agency is Assertiveness & Will to Take Control. Communion is Empathy & Compassion. Only the positive poles count, and cues are split into strong and weak.

The data are 45,000 German sentences, 15,000 each from Bundestag speeches, broadcast interviews and Facebook posts, covering 46 party leaders from 2017 to 2024. Few-shot prompting of DeepSeek-V3 and GPT-4o reaches macro-F1 0.74-0.77. Fine-tuned XLM-R reaches 0.70, bag-of-words SVM 0.55-0.63, and Llama 3-8B about 0.55-0.60. Human coders agree only moderately (alpha 0.70-0.78), and coders label 89-94% of sentences as having no cue. Strong-only definitions work better than strong plus weak. Only GPT-4o and DeepSeek pass the 18-unit functional test.

For external validity, communion share falls from left to right (LINKE 19% down to AfD and FDP about 6%). In the 2024 debate, Trump's cues were 63% agency and Harris's were 59% communion.

For Melange, this paper is the direct method source for `fec/members/agency_communion_llm.py`. That file copies the codebook, the positive-pole rule and the 18-unit test, and it reproduces the left-greater-than-right communion pattern (D .099 vs R .049). But the build departs from the paper in ways that matter:
- It uses a different model family (Claude Sonnet, in English).
- It keeps weak cues in the score.
- It samples only self-referential floor and hearing sentences, 40 per member.
- It has no human-labelled macro-F1 test set.

The paper says nothing to support the next step the system takes: turning projected persona into susceptibility to lobbying pressure. That mapping (.60 z(communion) − .40 z(agency) in the receptivity layer) is a design prior. Its one behavioural test so far (H4, +0.067 on Nokken-Poole drift) is below the threshold. The paper also gently undercuts the Ramey/Mairesse lexical lineage behind the Big Five reader.

paul_entries.citation: Birkenmaier & Lechner 2025, Political Analysis (agency and communion)

bearings.paper_claim: Few-shot LLM prompting with a theory-driven agency/communion codebook (positive poles only, strong vs weak cues) is the most valid strategy: DeepSeek-V3 macro-F1 0.77, GPT-4o 0.76 against human labels, and these two models alone pass all 18 functional test units.
bearings.system_side: agency_communion_llm.py takes the paper's construct definitions, the positive-pole rule, strong=1.0/weak=0.5 cue weights and the 18-unit functional test design (6 self-report, 6 opposite-pole, 6 unrelated). It runs Claude sonnet-5 (or fable) on English floor and hearing sentences. Its pass bar is >=16/18, and the brain records an 18/18 pass.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The construct and the test design carry over. The paper's validity numbers do not: they belong to GPT-4o/DeepSeek-V3 on German sentences sampled at natural base rates and scored against three trained coders. The system has no human-labelled sentence test for its own model and language, so its macro-F1 is unknown. The functional gate is the only part of the paper's validation it reproduces. Strength is strong for the method's lineage and weak for inherited accuracy.

bearings.paper_claim: Strong-only cue definitions performed better than strong plus weak (DeepSeek few-shot balanced 0.77 vs 0.76). Human coders label 94% (strong) and 89% (weak+strong) of sentences 'none'. Communion is higher on social media than in interviews, and female politicians show higher communion (App. M-N).
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 4.1, p.9; Sec. 5, p.14; footnote 12, p.13
bearings.system_side: The member score adds weak cues at 0.5 weight. The corpus is filtered to sentences containing I/we/my/our/me/us with ritual phrases removed, capped at 40 sentences per member (NSENT), and drawn only from the speeches table. The receptivity layer uses members with at least 15 classified sentences. agency_raw/communion_raw are written out, but nothing reports a strong-only score.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The self-reference filter changes the base rate, so the system's shares cannot be compared with the paper's percentages. Speech-only sampling makes the persona specific to one genre, and the paper shows genre shifts communion. Sex is not controlled. Whether a strong-only score would change member ordering can be tested from the cache at no cost, but nobody has run it. Moderate.

bearings.paper_claim: Party-level communion share falls steadily from left to right on both CHES dimensions: LINKE 19%, Greens 12%, SPD 10%, CDU 8%, AfD and FDP about 6%. Agency shows only a weak positive economic link.
bearings.system_side: The brain records the system's party signature, communion D .099 vs R .049, and the top communion members are progressive Democrats. It treats this as the construct-appropriate external check that passed at build time.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The comparison covers six German parties against a two-party US Congress. The direction replicates. Because the paper reports no coefficients, there is no magnitude to compare. A party gap is evidence of convergent validity, and it also means the score carries party. Under the brain rule, the pooled score is UNSTRATIFIED across the D/R fault line. Moderate.

bearings.paper_claim: The construct is projected public persona under the lens model. The authors say the weight of intrinsic personality versus strategic self-presentation cannot be determined. The paper tests no behavioural consequence: it does not link agency or communion to responsiveness, persuadability or legislative behaviour.
bearings.system_side: The receptivity layer folds persona into susceptibility as persona_susc_z = .60 z(communion) − .40 z(agency), blended at PERSONA_W 0.30 (the owner ruled to keep this). The z-scores pool all covered members across parties. Code comments read communion as approachable-agreeable (Byrne-susceptible) and agency as resistant to pressure.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports measuring the persona, but the communion→susceptibility link and the .60/.40 weights come from Byrne-style design priors, not from this paper. On the one well-powered behavioural test, persona's H4 was +0.067 on Nokken-Poole drift, right-signed but below the 0.094 permutation floor. Because the z-scores pool D and R, part of persona_z is a party shift. The engine already carries party through cpf. This is a scope note only; the PERSONA_W ruling stands and nothing here proposes removal.

bearings.paper_claim: Three coders working from a refined codebook reached only Krippendorff's alpha .70-.78 on a ternary sentence task, and no model exceeded macro-F1 0.80. Fuzzy constructs set the ceiling on precision.
bearings.system_side: The 2026-07-04 ruling relied on this floor. It judged the blind single-rater gold test (agency rho +0.035, communion −0.245, n=30) scope-mismatched, and it reopens persona validity only if a 3+ rater panel built to B&L standards fails.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The floor is for sentence-level ternary labels. The single-rater test used 1-9 holistic member scales, a different task, so the paper explains why that test was underpowered but does not certify the persona score. No panel to B&L standards has been run, so persona validity against human raters is still unestablished.

bearings.paper_claim: Ramey et al.'s use of a pretrained SVM (Mairesse) 'lacks validation against human-annotated data' and looks outdated. On their task, bag-of-words SVMs reach only 0.55-0.63 macro-F1 and fail the functional tests. The Big Five also offer little nuance specific to politics.

bearings.transfer_conditions: The critique hits harder here because the system's reference standard, RKH, is itself Mairesse/LIWC-derived, so convergence is method-shared. The paper's SVM numbers are for sentence classification, not member-level trait regression, so they do not directly measure this component's accuracy. Independent criteria such as the Senate panels are the evidence that counts.

bearings.paper_claim: LLM prompting succeeds at sentence-level classification of defined cues with a codebook and few-shot examples. Most sentences carry no cue (89-94% 'none').
bearings.system_side: The Pink reader rates 20 holistic Big Five items on de-identified chunks and codes 'cannot tell' as 0, citing cues being absent in about 90% of sentences. It failed its convergence bar (behavioural diagonal mean +0.064 < 0.12) and is display-only.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper validates a narrow, codebook-defined cue task, not holistic Big Five item rating, so its success does not transfer to Pink. The 'cannot tell'=0 design matches the paper's base rate. Weak.

gaps_exposed: The English Claude agency/communion instrument has no human-labelled sentence test set (3 coders, codebook, Krippendorff alpha, macro-F1). Only the 18-unit functional gate and the party signature are reproduced, so the paper's 0.74-0.77 cannot be claimed for this model.
No strong-only variant has been computed, although the paper found strong-only definitions more valid. The cache holds strength labels, so this costs nothing to compute.

Persona comes only from the speeches table (floor and hearings), with self-referential filtering and 40 sentences per member. The paper shows communion differs by source (higher on social media), and the system has no per-genre persona estimate.

persona_susc_z is z-scored across parties together (receptivity_layer.py:152-155), even though both the paper and the system show a party gap in communion. There is no within-party standardization and no sex control (the paper reports higher communion for female politicians).
Persona is a static snapshot. The paper flags role transitions (becoming chair or lead candidate) and crises as drivers of displayed personality, and no time window or change tracking exists.

There is no audit for partisan or pretraining bias in the LLM classifier, which the paper recommends for political content. The party signature alone cannot separate a real party difference from model bias.
flags: UNSTRATIFIED: persona_susc_z pools D and R in its z-scores (fec/members/receptivity_layer.py:152-155) across a fault line that both the paper and the system's own party signature (D .099 vs R .049) show. Any figure quoting a persona effect must carry the UNSTRATIFIED label or be split by party.

extraction.title: Measuring Elite Personality Using Speech
extraction.document_type: Journal article (empirical; measurement method plus validity checks and one substantive application)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all of _text/5e248be1ab0d.txt (about 1,630 lines; body, footnotes, Tables 1-3, figure notes, references). Annotation file _annots/5e248be1ab0d.json read in full: 69 highlights, all by Paul Goff, zero sticky notes or typed notes. Metadata hint is correct; no correction needed.
extraction.research_question: Can Big Five personality traits of US legislators be measured from floor speech text without surveys, and are the resulting estimates valid and substantively useful? Specifically: (a) do text-based estimates parallel known personality-ideology links, (b) do survey nonresponse rates depend on personality, and (c) does Conscientiousness predict the share of symbolic/ceremonial bills proposed, conditional on majority status.
extraction.theory: Big Five (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Emotional Stability) personality is related to political behavior and ideology (Gerber et al. 2010, 2011a; Mondak 2010; Jost, Nosek and Gosling 2008). Survey inventories suffer from low response and social desirability, so personality should be inferred from language (Mairesse et al. 2007). Expected ideology signs: Openness, Conscientiousness and Emotional Stability negative toward liberalism; Agreeableness negative to Common Space score; Extraversion agnostic. Symbolic-bill hypothesis: Conscientious legislators propose fewer ceremonial bills because they are goal-oriented and persist against partisan hurdles (Cox and McCubbins 2005; Aldrich 1995); the effect should be larger for the minority, where free-riding on majority leadership is unavailable. Authors also argue Conscientiousness acts as a discount factor (fn 35).
extraction.data: Sources: Congressional Record floor speeches by every sitting House member, 104th-113th Congresses (1996-2014). Unit of measurement: member-year (scores estimated per year, then jackknifed across years). Sample for personality scores: all incumbent House members in the period; the paper does not report total speech counts. Table 1: N = 844 House members (lifetime mean personality, 1996-2014 Common Space). Table 2: NPAT response, N = 598 members (622 in Model 1), pooled by member. Table 3: House bills proposed in 104th-112th Congresses, binomial logit at member-Congress level, N = 3,648 (Models 3-5; 3,736 and 3,732 in Models 1-2). Training data for the pre-trained model: Pennebaker and King (1999) essays (~1.9 million words) and Mehl, Gosling and Pennebaker (2006) conversations (~100,000 words), per Mairesse et al. (2007). Median member uttered ~11,000 words per year (p.7).
extraction.method: Pre-trained Mairesse et al. (2007) SMOreg (SVM regression, Weka) applied to LIWC (2001) and MRCPD features, standardized, in corpus mode: (1) process each member-year's speeches through LIWC and MRCPD; (2) apply the standardized SMOreg models; (3) save Big Five estimates per year; (4) optional jackknife (average of all other years) to reduce language tied to same-year actions; (5) uncertainty from 100 sentence-level bootstrap replications per member-year (Lowe and Benoit 2011), 95% CIs. Scores are on a 1-7 scale and relative to the Congressional Record, not comparable to general-population inventories (fn 10). Validity is indirect: (a) OLS of Common Space scores on lifetime trait means with demographics (Table 1); (b) yearly correlations of traits with LIWC features (Fig 4); (c) authorship/speechwriter checks (Pelosi, Boehner, Ron Paul; p.11); (d) logistic regression of ever responding to NPAT on traits and controls (Table 2, Fig 5); (e) binomial logit of ceremonial-bill share with Majority Party x trait interactions and Congress FE in Model 5 (Table 3, Fig 6). Bill classification follows Volden and Wiseman (2014) title keywords.
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. The authors explicitly refrain from claiming causal priority between personality and ideology (fn 20, p.9). Jackknife correction (step 4, p.5) is presented as alleviating endogeneity from same-year action language. The NPAT and bill analyses are conditional associations; the bill model adds party interactions and (Model 5) Congress fixed effects. Selection into survey response is treated as a confound to be shown empirically rather than solved.
extraction.scope: Population: incumbent US House members, 1996-2014 (104th-113th Congress) for personality scores; bill analysis covers House bills in 104th-112th Congresses. Institution: US House floor speech (Congressional Record). Era: post-1996 only; pre-1996 Record not digitized (p.19). Excludes Senate, challengers, state legislators, and presidents (presidents discussed only in an argument, p.11-12). The paper states the method may generalize to other text sources but these are not tested.

key_findings.finding: Text-based Big Five estimates are stable and precise for incumbent House members over time; uncertainty shrinks with word count.
key_findings.numbers: Median member ~11,000 words/year. Above ~5,000 words, CI width about 0.3 or less (point estimate +/-0.15 on 1-7 scale). Average CI width ~0.35 (+/-0.175).

key_findings.finding: Congressional floor speech LIWC category usage closely matches the Pennebaker laboratory corpus used to train the model, so the transfer is judged acceptable.
key_findings.numbers: Correlation ~0.99 on untransformed scale; Kendall tau-B = 0.72 for rank orderings (p<0.001).

key_findings.finding: Personality estimates show the expected relationships with Common Space ideology; the model explains only a modest share of ideology variance.
key_findings.numbers: N = 844. Model 1: Openness -0.26***, Conscientiousness 0.26***, Extraversion -0.15***, Agreeableness -0.17**, Emotional Stability 0.20***; R2 = 0.10. Model 4 (with Female and Birth Year): R2 = 0.16, all four expected-sign traits significant (Agreeableness at p<0.05 in Model 4).

key_findings.finding: Emotional Stability predicts response to the National Political Awareness Test (NPAT), indicating survey-based elite personality measures suffer selection bias.
key_findings.numbers: N = 598 (622 in Model 1). Emotional Stability: 0.47* (M1), 0.49* (M2), 0.62** (M3), 0.58** (M4, SE 0.28). Moving Emotional Stability from -2 SD to +2 SD raises predicted response probability from about 30% to about 53% (Model 4).

key_findings.finding: Conscientiousness reduces the share of ceremonial/symbolic bills proposed, and this effect is smaller for majority-party members.
key_findings.numbers: Conscientiousness: -0.52*** (M1), -0.39*** (M3), -0.53*** (M4), -0.58*** (M5, with Congress FE). Majority Party x Conscientiousness: +0.27** (M4), +0.29*** (M5). Majority Party x Extraversion: -0.33*** (M4). N = 3,648 (M3-M5). Authors: Conscientiousness affects majority members least (p.17-18); minority members must be highly Conscientious to propose substantive bills.

key_findings.finding: Speechwriter concern is judged a non-issue: estimates stay stable through Speaker changes and across members with and without speechwriters.
key_findings.numbers: Speechwriters not hired by most members per House disbursement records (qualitative). Pelosi and Boehner estimates stable even though neither was Speaker at the start of the data.

key_findings.finding: Text-based validity checks support the measure, but the paper provides no direct validation against a ground-truth personality inventory for legislators.
key_findings.numbers: None; validity is indirect (ideology correlations, LIWC face validity, NPAT, bills).

limitations: Strategic misrepresentation: legislators may adopt false personas or speech patterns that are known to listeners and voluntarily controllable (p.7-8). Authors argue this would attenuate, not invalidate, results.
Validity is indirect only; no direct ground-truth personality measure for legislators exists (p.6-7).
Scores are relative to the Congressional Record and not comparable to general-population inventories such as the TIPI (fn 10, p.4).
Training corpus is nonpolitical lab essays and conversations; similar LIWC category usage does not establish similar word use (p.3, fn 10).
Self-selection of members into elected office makes their trait distribution differ from the general population (fn 10, p.4).
Speechwriter effects are assumed small based on disbursement records and a Reagan analogy; not directly tested for most members (p.11-12).
Missing data: survey-based approaches fail under MAR assumption when missingness depends on personality (p.12).
NPAT response is a low bar, which biases against finding significant results (p.13); the outcome is ever-response only, with member-level means.
Ron Paul example and face validity rely on the authors' interpretations of trait stereotypes (p.5).
Causal direction between personality and ideology is not resolved (fn 20, p.9).
Pre-1996 Congressional Record not digitized; estimates not available for earlier periods (p.19).
Other text sources (challengers, social media, press releases) not tested; comparability unknown (p.18, fn 39).
Yearly estimation chosen partly for computing constraints; Congress-level estimates would take weeks to months (fn 11, p.4).

summary_md:
Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh (PSRM 2016) score Big Five traits for every sitting House member from 1996 to 2014. They run each member-year of Congressional Record floor speech through LIWC and MRC features, then through Mairesse et al.'s pre-trained SMOreg models. Scores sit on a 1-7 scale that is relative to the Record. The method adds an optional leave-one-year-out jackknife and 100 sentence-level bootstrap replications per member-year. Above about 5,000 words a year, confidence intervals narrow to about ±0.15. The paper never validates directly against a personality inventory. Its validity evidence is indirect:
- Lifetime trait means relate to Common Space ideology with the expected signs, but explain only R2 = 0.10 (N = 844).
- Emotional Stability predicts whether a member ever answered the NPAT. Predicted response rises from about 30% to about 53% between -2 SD and +2 SD (N = 598).
- Conscientiousness lowers the share of ceremonial bills a member sponsors (-0.39 to -0.58; N = 3,648 member-Congresses, 104th-112th). A positive Majority × C interaction (+0.27 to +0.29) puts most of that effect in the minority party.

This is the template for Melange's lexical Big Five. fec/members/big5_traits.py names the paper and copies its steps. lep_criterion.py runs the Table 3 ceremonial-share test as its paper-exact C criterion. The test came back null for all three C measures: rho between +0.000 and +0.018, n = 440 members, 115th-118th Congresses pooled, at least 8 sponsored bills each. That run did not split majority from minority, the fault line the paper says carries the effect, so the null is UNSTRATIFIED. The paper also gives no grounds for treating the published RKH scores as ground truth. They come from the same Mairesse-LIWC family, which is why the system's convergence against them is inflated by shared method. Finally, the paper's speechwriter defence covers floor speech only. It does not cover the tweets and interviews the system pools in.

bearings.paper_claim: Big Five scored per member-year by the pre-trained Mairesse SMOreg on standardized LIWC and MRCPD features from floor speech. Scores are relative to the Congressional Record (fn 10). Uncertainty comes from 100 sentence-level bootstraps per member-year, and CI width is about 0.3 or less above about 5,000 words a year. The median member speaks about 11,000 words a year. An optional jackknife averages the other years to strip language tied to same-year actions.
bearings.system_side: The code reproduces the steps: closed-vocabulary rates are corpus-standardized, fed into a linear or SMOreg weight file, and the trait z-scores are re-standardized relative to this corpus. Three steps differ from the paper. (1) Text is pooled across genres (CREC plus INTERVIEW by default, with social posts available), with no per-year estimation and no jackknife. (2) There is no bootstrap CI. A lowconf flag below 1,500 tokens replaces it, and consumers shrink scores toward 0. (3) Weights are refit to the published RKH scores per trait, giving held-out CV mean r = .350. The party-sign check codes Extraversion as expected -1, but the paper stays agnostic on Extraversion.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The pipeline transfers as a procedure. The precision numbers do not. They assume single-genre floor speech per member-year at about 11,000 words, while the system's 1,500-token floor is well below the paper's 5,000-word precision band. The jackknife's endogeneity protection is absent because the system has no time slicing outside the BIG5_BEFORE/AFTER validation hooks. Refitting to RKH makes the system share the paper's method rather than validate against it.

bearings.paper_claim: Conscientiousness lowers the ceremonial share of sponsored bills: -0.52*** (M1), -0.39*** (M3), -0.53*** (M4) and -0.58*** (M5, with Congress fixed effects). Majority × C is +0.27** (M4) and +0.29*** (M5), so the effect is smallest in the majority. N = 3,648 member-Congresses, 104th-112th, binomial logit weighted by bills.
bearings.system_side: lep_criterion.py treats this as the 'paper-exact RKH C criterion'. It computes Spearman rho between each member's pooled ceremonial share (115th-118th Congresses, at least 8 bills) and diligence_z, lexical C v1 and behaviour-calibrated C v2. The stored results in data/members/lep_criterion.json are rho +0.003, +0.018 and +0.000 (n = 440, all null). The test does not split by majority status and does not weight by number of bills.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's effect sits in minority-party members. A rank correlation pooled over majority and minority members is therefore an UNSTRATIFIED test of a conditional claim. Modern Congresses also carry few ceremonial bills, and the script itself flags that this attenuates the test (lines 125-128). The null is not evidence against RKH until the test is re-run stratified by majority status and weighted by bill count. Any such re-run is new analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper's only behavioural Conscientiousness criterion is the ceremonial-bill share (Table 3). It does not analyse roll-call participation anywhere.
bearings.paper_location: pp.15-18, Table 3 (measures list: no votes-cast outcome)
bearings.system_side: The docstring labels diligence_z (roll-call participation) as 'RKH's strongest C criterion'. Diligence is now the mean of participation and LEP follow-through, meaning committee-action-and-beyond stage events per bill introduced.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a citation error, not a modelling error. lep_criterion.py:7 already records that an earlier RKH criterion (committee chair) was mis-sourced. The follow-through component is closer to the paper's substantive-versus-symbolic logic. The participation component has no support in RKH and should be cited to its real source.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper has no direct validation against a ground-truth personality measure for legislators. Its validity rests on ideology correlations, LIWC face validity, NPAT response and bill shares. Its own NPAT result shows that self-report surveys of elites are selection-biased by trait: Emotional Stability raises predicted response from about 30% to about 53%.
bearings.system_side: The system validates against independent Senate expert and insider panels using pre-registered single looks. It treats convergence with RKH as method-shared and therefore inflated. E and A pass both panels, O passes academics only, N passes insiders only, and C shows only an insider association.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The NPAT argument is about self-report non-response. It does not apply to expert ratings, so the system's panels avoid the bias the paper documents. The panels are Senate and the paper is House, so cross-chamber transfer is assumed rather than shown. The external RKH criterion is 15-25 years old and range-restricted (n = 147 overlapping members).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Big Five validation against Senate gold panels and criteria|Big Five validation against Senate gold panels and criteria]]

bearings.paper_claim: Emotional Stability has the weakest face-validity link: its link to anxiety words is 'somewhat weaker' than the other traits' one-feature links. ES still predicts survey response and loads positively on conservatism (0.20***, Table 1 M1).
bearings.system_side: N = -ES is carried over from the paper. Affective N is E- and party-residualized and correlates only -0.11 raw (-0.04 with E removed, not significant) with RKH-ES. The broader text-N reaches -0.22. Interview-to-floor genre transfer failed (rho .050 and .161).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's weak ES-anxiety link is consistent with the system's finding that a narrow affective facet does not recover the RKH ES estimate. Party-residualizing removes the ideology covariance that RKH reports, so the paper's ES may partly carry partisan signal.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests|Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests]]

bearings.paper_claim: Conscientiousness behaves like a discount factor, meaning more weight on future payoffs (fn 35). Its behavioural effect depends on majority status: minority members need high C to persist against partisan hurdles, while majority members are least affected.
bearings.system_side: susc_trait takes -.20 × diligence on the behavioural basis and -.20 × C on the lexical basis. Both bases apply the term unconditionally, with no majority-status interaction. The sign is a design prior, not an estimate.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper concerns bill-type choice, not response to lobbying pressure, so the transfer is analogical. If adopted, the C term would be conditioned on majority status. That is only a proposal: the lep_criterion null and the receptivity validity record (H1/H2 underpowered) give no evidence for any C-pressure link today.

gaps_exposed: No per-year estimation and no leave-one-year-out jackknife: lexical Big Five pools all available text, so trait scores can carry language tied to the same actions they are later used to predict (diligence, sponsorship).

No bootstrap uncertainty on trait scores: a binary lowconf flag at 1,500 tokens replaces the sentence-level bootstrap CIs, and 1,500 tokens is well below the paper's roughly 5,000-word precision band.

The RKH ceremonial-share criterion is pooled across majority and minority members and is not bill-weighted. The paper's effect is minority-concentrated (Majority × C +0.27 to +0.29), so the stored null (n = 440, 115th-118th) is UNSTRATIFIED and cannot refute or confirm it.

Genre mixing (CREC, interviews, social) has no counterpart to the paper's speechwriter defence. The defence rests on House disbursement records for floor speech and does not cover staff-run social accounts.
Weights refit to RKH targets make RKH convergence (held-out CV mean r = .350) a fit statistic, not validation. The paper offers no ground-truth anchor that would rescue it.
flags: Mis-citation: behavioral_dispositions.py:13-14 calls roll-call participation "RKH's strongest C criterion", but the paper has no participation analysis. Its C criterion is the ceremonial-bill share. This is the second RKH mis-sourcing, after the committee-chair criterion recorded at lep_criterion.py:7.

Pooled-coefficient rule: any quote of the lep_criterion ceremonial-share result must carry the label UNSTRATIFIED (no majority/minority split), with window 115th-118th and denominator n = 440 members with at least 8 sponsored bills.

The paper's own claim of 'superiority of text-based measurement' (highlighted by Paul) is not established for this system. The system's RKH-referenced convergence is method-shared, and its pre-registered panel looks MISSed several improvement rounds. External claims need status labels per the brain discipline.
big5_traits.py:276 hard-codes an expected Extraversion sign of -1. The paper explicitly stays agnostic on Extraversion (p.9), so a 'REVERSED' verdict on E is not a paper-based failure.
paul_alignment: Paul's position calls Ramey 'dated but foundational' and asks for frameworks specific to each venue. That matches what the system built: a step-by-step synthesis of Ramey, then a Birkenmaier-motivated move to LLM and behavioural readers, with genre-transfer tests that failed for N. Paul has highlighted, in pink and violet, the claims that 'measurement of elite personality is possible' and that 'the Big Five do indeed play a role in legislative decisionmaking'. He also highlighted Conscientiousness's minority-party effect on sponsorship. The system's own record is more sceptical. The paper-exact C criterion came back null on the current roster (UNSTRATIFIED, n = 440, 115th-118th), lexical C reversed on roll-call participation, and the receptivity layer moved to a behavioural basis. Paul's notes on the legislative pillar and on behavioural dispositions cite Ramey for 'conscientiousness relates to sponsorship'. That note is stale: the system tested the link and found nothing. Paul's minority-party highlight points to the one untested refinement, a run stratified by majority status. His SSRN-citation annotation entry has no takeaways or system links, so nothing in it conflicts.

related.why: Birkenmaier criticizes Ramey's SVM-on-LIWC approach as outdated and not validated against human coding, and validates LLM readers instead. The system's move to the Pink LLM reader and the agency/communion persona follows that critique.
Expert ratings of senators supply the direct ground truth that Ramey says does not exist. These are the system's gold panels.

Supplies the trait-to-pressure mechanism that the receptivity layer hangs on Ramey-style trait scores.
Uses politician personality to predict a behavioural outcome (media visibility), a parallel to Ramey's substantive application.
PoliPers separates ideal from actual politician personality. That speaks to Ramey's strategic-misrepresentation limitation.

backlinks.why: Ramey links conscientiousness to sponsorship. Fouirnaies & Hall show sponsorship and participation also move with electoral incentive inside the same person, a situational confound for any trait reading of those behaviours (diligence_z, the C criterion).
Text-based elite personality from speech, the legislator-side basis of the lexical-big5 instrument that Marrero's linguistic block parallels in students.

Both measure elites from speech. Ramey reads traits from words, while Dietrich argues words are strategic and pitch less so. This is the text-versus-voice tension behind the lexical Big Five and audio lanes.
The system's lexical reader copies Ramey's pipeline for legislators. The survey covers the general-population ML lineage, which does not address elites.

extraction.document_type: Theoretical computer science preprint (algorithm design and worst-case analysis)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 960 lines of _text/203c3d9d4ab6.txt (51,509 chars), in chunks, through the references (pp. 1-17). All 26 annotation items in _annots/203c3d9d4ab6.json were read; the file contains one JSON array only. Metadata hint was correct on title and authors (author order matches). Year 2025 confirmed. extraction.research_question: Can single-source shortest paths (SSSP) on directed graphs with real non-negative edge weights be solved faster than Dijkstra's O(m + n log n) bound on sparse graphs, in the comparison-addition model, and can the Omega(n log n) sorting barrier be broken for this problem?
extraction.theory: Dijkstra's algorithm sorts vertices by distance through a priority queue, which costs Theta(n log n) on the frontier. Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges in k rounds with no sorting. The paper merges the two ideas through recursive partitioning, in the style of bottleneck-path algorithms (Gabow-Tarjan 1988; Chechik et al. 2016; Duan et al. 2018), so that the frontier is shrunk to pivots before any sorting (pp. 2-4). The sorting cost is reduced by a block-based partial-sorting structure (Lemma 3.3, pp. 6-7). The paper does not present a behavioural or social theory.
extraction.data: No empirical data. The analysis is over worst-case inputs: directed graph G=(V,E) with n vertices, m edges, and non-negative real weights w: E to R>=0. The algorithm first transforms G into a constant-degree graph G' with O(m) vertices and O(m) edges via zero-weight cycles (Sec. 2, p. 3). The bound assumes m = O(n) (p. 4). No sample, N, or time period applies.
extraction.method: Deterministic algorithm design plus worst-case running-time analysis. The core procedure is a recursive bounded multi-source shortest path routine, BMSSP(l, B, S) (Algorithm 3, p. 10). It uses FindPivots (Algorithm 1, p. 6), a base case that is a mini-Dijkstra (Algorithm 2, p. 9), and a partial-sort block-list data structure D (Lemma 3.3, pp. 6-8). Parameters are k = floor(log^(1/3) n) and t = floor(log^(2/3) n), with recursion depth ceil(log n / t) (Sec. 3.1, p. 4). Correctness is proved by induction on level l (Lemma 3.7, pp. 12-13). Time is bounded in Lemma 3.12 (p. 14).
extraction.identification: Not applicable. This is a worst-case complexity result, not a statistical or causal identification strategy.
extraction.scope: Population: directed graphs with real non-negative weights, sparse regime m = O(n) after a constant-degree transformation. Model: comparison-addition only (each addition and comparison takes unit time; no other operations on weights). Era: 2025 arXiv preprint. Institutions: Tsinghua University, Stanford University, and Max Planck Institute for Informatics (author affiliations, p. 2 footnotes). The paper does not address lobbying, networks as social objects, elections, persuasion, turnout, legislators, or text measurement.

key_findings.finding: Main result: a deterministic SSSP algorithm for directed graphs with real non-negative weights in time O(m log^(2/3) n), the first to break the O(m + n log n) bound of Dijkstra on sparse graphs.
key_findings.numbers: O(m log^(2/3) n)

key_findings.finding: The result is also the first deterministic algorithm to beat O(m + n log n) for SSSP even on undirected graphs, since the prior O(m sqrt(log n log log n)) SSSP algorithm of Duan, Mao, Shu, Yin (DMSY23) is randomized.
key_findings.location: Sec. 1, p. 2 (remark after Theorem 1.1); DMSY23 cited on p. 1
key_findings.numbers: DMSY23: O(m sqrt(log n log log n)) randomized, undirected

key_findings.finding: Dijkstra is optimal if the output must include the vertex ordering by distance (Haeupler et al. 2024), so the improvement applies to distances without a full ordering.
key_findings.location: Sec. 1, p. 1 (citing HHR+24); Sec. 3.1 p. 4 ('without necessarily recovering a complete ordering')

key_findings.finding: Key idea: shrink the frontier. For a bound B, the frontier S is reduced to pivots of size at most |eU|/k, where k = log^(Omega(1)) n. Each pivot roots a shortest-path tree of at least k vertices.
key_findings.location: Technical overview, Sec. 1.1, p. 2; FindPivots Lemma 3.2, p. 5
key_findings.numbers: |W| = O(k|S|); |P| <= |W|/k <= |eU|/k; time O(min{k^2|S|, k|eU|})

key_findings.finding: Per-vertex running time is reduced from Theta(log n) to log n / log^(Omega(1)) n through divide-and-conquer over log n / t levels.
key_findings.numbers: log n / log^(Omega(1))(n) per vertex

key_findings.finding: Parameter choice that yields the final bound: k = floor(log^(1/3) n), t = floor(log^(2/3) n), recursion level l = ceil(log n / t).
key_findings.location: Sec. 3.1, p. 4; Lemma 3.12 final statement, p. 14
key_findings.numbers: k = floor(log^(1/3) n); t = floor(log^(2/3) n); l = ceil(log n / t)

key_findings.finding: Output-size bound for each BMSSP call: the returned set U has size at most 4k^(2lt), and a partial run has |U| at least k^(2lt).
key_findings.numbers: |U| <= 4k^(2lt); partial case |U| >= k^(2lt)

limitations: Theoretical only. The text reports no implementation or experiments, so practical constants are unmeasured. The hidden constant C in the bounds is not quantified.

Computation model is the comparison-addition model only (real weights; each addition and comparison costs unit time). Integer-weight or word-RAM improvements are discussed as related work (Thorup 1999/2004), not as this paper's result.

Assumes constant in- and out-degree via a transformation (Sec. 2, p. 3). The transformation is stated to preserve shortest paths and yield O(m) vertices and edges. Assumes m >= n-1 and every vertex reachable from s (p. 3-4).
Assumes all path lengths are distinct (Assumption 2.1, p. 4). The paper argues a lexicographic tuple order makes this WLOG, using Pred[] and hop count alpha stored per bd[v] (p. 4).

Bound is O(m log^(2/3) n), which is superlinear on sparse graphs; the paper does not claim linear time. The result is for distances and does not produce the full distance ordering. The paper cites HHR+24 that Dijkstra is optimal if ordering is required (p. 1).
Partial executions of BMSSP are noted as more complex to analyze, and the paper introduces batch-prepend and FindPivots to handle them (Sec. 3.1, p. 5; Lemma 3.3, p. 7).

summary_md:
Duan, Mao, Mao, Shu and Yin (arXiv 2504.17033v2, 2025; Paul's bib lists it as STOC 2025) give a deterministic single-source shortest-path algorithm for **directed** graphs with real non-negative weights that runs in O(m log^(2/3) n) in the comparison-addition model. It is the first to beat Dijkstra's O(m + n log n) on sparse graphs. The method combines Dijkstra with Bellman-Ford through a recursive bounded multi-source routine (BMSSP). FindPivots shrinks the frontier to at most |U|/k pivots, and a block-list structure sorts only partially, with k = log^(1/3) n and t = log^(2/3) n. The result covers distances only, with no full distance ordering. It is purely theoretical: there is no implementation, and the constant C is never given.

For Paul's systems this is a speed result with very little to transfer. Every route engine as built is either tiny (533 members, an O(N^2) array scan in the dashboard), a point-to-sink query that stops early (staffer closeness routes, bidirectional, plus Yen alternatives), or an integer-weight search (overlap routes). The paper's bound covers full single-source distances on sparse graphs with real weights, so none of these uses fits its model. The one real link is Assumption 2.1: the paper breaks ties by lexicographic order on (length, hop count, predecessor), which matches the staffer router's (cost, steps) tie rule. On latency, the staffer-network lane found the bottleneck was memory (pair_cache), not the heap's log n. ALT landmarks remain the deferred lever, and this paper does not replace them. While checking the dashboard's 'provably optimal' chain, I found a possible problem with edge direction (see flags). It is UNVERIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: O(m log^(2/3) n) beats Dijkstra only for single-source distances to ALL vertices, on sparse directed graphs (m = O(n) after a constant-degree transform), in the comparison-addition model. It returns distances without a full ordering. Dijkstra stays optimal when the ordering is required (HHR+24). The hidden constant C is not quantified and nothing is implemented.
bearings.paper_location: Theorem 1.1, p. 1; Sec. 1, p. 1 (HHR+24); Sec. 2-3.1, pp. 3-4; Lemma 3.12, p. 14
bearings.system_side: The default office route is a point-to-sink search. It is bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0 that stops once the frontier lower bounds pass the best meeting point. A second pass computes in exact integers, by scaling dyadic floats, and Yen's loopless alternatives need repeated shortest-path calls. On 2026-10-02 the latency cause was diagnosed as memory: pair_cache grew the sidecar from 7.0 to 17.5 GB. It was not heap cost. ALT landmarks are deferred.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The bound carries over only if the system ever needs full single-source distance fields over the ~4.66M-pair staffer graph, for example one origin to every office. Even then, the theoretical gain at n ~ 10^6-10^7 is about log n / log^(2/3) n, roughly 2.5-3x before an unknown constant. It does not carry over to early-stopping point-to-point queries, bidirectional search, Yen alternatives, or exact-tie passes, and it does not touch the measured memory bottleneck. Treat it as no recommendation to change the router.

bearings.paper_claim: Assumption 2.1 makes all path lengths distinct without loss of generality by comparing lexicographic tuples (length, hop count alpha, predecessor sequence), stored per bd[v] with Pred[].
bearings.system_side: Routes are keyed by (cost, steps). Costs within 1e-12 relative count as ties, and then fewest steps wins, then least exact cost, then the smallest node ids read from the sink end (Paul's 2026-10-03 tie ruling, D-082).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The (length, hops, then node id) order is the standard tie-breaker in algorithm theory, so it is not ad hoc, and any future algorithm that assumes distinct path lengths can keep it. The paper's comparisons are exact. The system's 1e-12 relative tie band is a separate tolerance that the paper does not cover.

paul_alignment: Paul's two bibliography entries for this paper carry citations only, with no takeaways. His 26 highlights mark the headline claim, the Dijkstra/Bellman-Ford contrast, the frontier-shrinking idea and the comparison-addition model, so he read it as algorithm background. His stated path-finding gaps are not addressed here: he wants to turn lobbying and bipartite data into a routable graph and to use A* heuristics that cope with unstable information. This paper speeds up exact SSSP. It says nothing about graph construction, heuristics, dynamic replanning or probabilistic reliability. His notes are not stale, but the system has since moved on. The 2026-10-02 staffer-latency lane showed the routers are bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0, that the bottleneck was memory rather than sorting, and that ALT is deferred. A theoretical sorting-barrier result therefore has no current place in the build. Citing Duan under member-recruitment-path is accurate only as background.
